passage:
I'm Gurpreet. I sit next to Hafsa in the hostel study room, so I saw how it started.
On Tuesday Hafsa got a text: Your scholarship KYC is pending. Update in 2 hrs or payment stops, with a link. She didn't tap it. She frowned, opened the university portal herself, and found nothing pending.
Then she did something I wouldn't have thought of. She took a screenshot, crossed out the link in red, and posted it in our class group: Fake. Don't click. Check the portal directly. She reported the number on the cybercrime portal too, and sent the same screenshot to her family group with a voice note in Urdu for her grandmother.
By evening, three people in our class said they had got it too. I forwarded Hafsa's warning to my Nani. She called me that night. She had received a similar message about her pension and hadn't known what to do.

qa.q: Where did Hafsa check whether her KYC was pending?
qa.a: She opened the university portal herself and found nothing pending.

qa.q: What does Hafsa's frown suggest when the text arrived?
qa.a: It suggests she felt suspicious of the urgent deadline and link rather than panicked.

qa.q: Which of Hafsa's steps protected the most people?
qa.a: Posting a marked screenshot with a clear warning to the class and family groups, including a voice note for her grandmother, spread the alert to people less used to such tricks.

qa.q: What was it like for Gurpreet's Nani to get the warning?
qa.a: Nani was relieved, having received a similar pension message without knowing what to do.

grounding: A student who spots a fake scholarship message checks the official portal, reports it and warns her class and family, and the warning reaches an older relative in time.

passage:
Monday. Damini, three months into her first job, got an email that seemed to come from the office IT team: Mailbox full. Log in here within 24 hours. The sender's address ended in a strange domain. She reported it with the phishing button and forgot about it.
Wednesday. At lunch, Devika from accounts, who is close to retirement and still prints her emails, mentioned a mailbox-full warning she planned to deal with after tea. Damini put down her fork. "Can I look at it with you first?" Same strange domain. They reported it together, and Damini posted a short note in the team chat: Fake IT emails going around. Check the sender. When in doubt, call IT on the extension.
Friday. IT sent an office-wide alert. Four people had received the email; nobody had logged in. Devika stopped by Damini's desk with a box of homemade laddoos. "For the warning," she said.

qa.q: What did the fake email tell Damini to do?
qa.a: It said Mailbox full. Log in here within 24 hours.

qa.q: Why did Damini put down her fork at lunch?
qa.a: She was alarmed, recognising the fake email she had reported and worried Devika would log in after tea.

qa.q: What made Damini's warning in the team chat useful?
qa.a: It was short and practical: check the sender, and when in doubt call IT on the extension, so less experienced email users knew exactly what to do.

qa.q: How did Devika feel about Damini's help?
qa.a: Devika felt grateful, bringing homemade laddoos to thank Damini for the warning.

grounding: A young employee reports a phishing email, spots it again in Devika's inbox and warns the whole team, so no one logs in.
